questions.q: What is the actual division of labor between Python and compiled languages (C, C++, Fortran) in a typical quantum software stack?
options: Python handles describing and orchestrating what a circuit does (the control layer), while compiled libraries or hardware electronics handle the heavy numerical computation or real-time control
Python performs all the numerical linear algebra itself, with no compiled code involved anywhere
Compiled languages are only used for drawing circuit diagrams, never for computation
Python and compiled languages are never both involved in the same quantum program
questions.explain: Python is used almost universally as the control layer -- building circuit objects, calling run(), inspecting results -- while the performance-critical linear algebra or hardware control happens in compiled code that Python calls into.

questions.q: Why doesn't NumPy's matrix-vector multiplication suffer from Python's reputation for being slow?
options: Because an operation like `H @ psi0` calls into BLAS/LAPACK, compiled linear algebra libraries, so the actual element-by-element work happens outside the Python interpreter entirely
Because NumPy secretly rewrites Python into C before every operation
Because Python's interpreter is actually fast for loops, contrary to its reputation
Because the Hadamard gate is a special case that NumPy optimizes differently from other matrices
questions.explain: The rule is to push the loop into NumPy rather than write it in Python -- a vectorized call like `H @ psi0` hands the real looping work to decades-old, highly optimized BLAS/LAPACK code, bypassing the slow part of the Python interpreter.

questions.q: In the lesson's NumPy example, the Hadamard gate is applied to the state |0>. What probabilities result from measuring the resulting state, and why?
options: 0.5 and 0.5, because both amplitudes come out to 1/sqrt(2) and squaring each magnitude gives an equal 50/50 split between measuring 0 and 1
1.0 and 0.0, because the Hadamard gate leaves |0> completely unchanged
0.36 and 0.64, because that is the general result of any single-qubit gate
It cannot be determined without running the code, since NumPy's output is random
questions.explain: H|0> produces amplitudes of 1/sqrt(2) (about 0.70710678) in both positions; squaring each magnitude gives 0.5 and 0.5, the signature equal superposition the Hadamard gate is defined to produce.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three general-purpose scientific Python libraries the lesson identifies as the non-framework-specific foundation for quantum computing work?
options: Qiskit
NumPy
SciPy
Matplotlib
questions.explain: Qiskit is a quantum-specific SDK built on top of the general numerical stack, not a general-purpose scientific library itself. NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib are the three general-purpose libraries the lesson names as the common foundation underneath every quantum SDK.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why does Chapter 1 focus on plain Python and NumPy before introducing any quantum-specific SDK like Qiskit?
options: Because every quantum SDK assumes the programmer is already fluent with arrays, classes, and functions before calling into framework-specific objects like a QuantumCircuit
Because quantum SDKs are being deprecated in favor of plain NumPy
Because Qiskit, Cirq, and PennyLane do not actually use Python internally
Because this course will never use a quantum SDK at any point
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states the point of Chapter 1 is making sure the plain Python and NumPy skills underneath every SDK are solid first, since frameworks like Qiskit build directly on that foundation.
